# The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being **rearrested within three years**. The department has two proposed uses:

- **Use A:** people above a threshold get **more restrictive supervision** (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
- **Use B:** people above a threshold get **priority for reentry services** (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model **will not use race**. You've been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

**What you're turning in:** this rendered document, published in the `assignments/` folder of your portfolio.

**How this assignment works:** it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The **Week 11 lab** (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

| A6 part | Week 11 lab step |
|---|---|
| 3.1 odds ratios | Step 3 |
| 4.1 predictions + confusion matrix | Steps 4–5 |
| 4.3 threshold sweep | Step 5 (`rates_at()`) |
| 4.4 ROC + AUC | Step 6 |
| 5.1–5.2 errors by race | Step 7 |
| 5.3 what carries race in | Step 8 |

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called **`recid`** (not `two_year_recid`), and you **fit on `train` and evaluate on `test`**. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every `predict()` in Parts 4 and 5 needs `newdata = test`.


# The data

The National Institute of Justice's **Recidivism Forecasting Challenge** data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Following the updated announcement, I downloaded **Full dataset (csv)** from the [NIJ website](https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/recidivism-forecasting-challenge) and saved it as `data/assignment6/nij_recidivism.csv` for this working copy.

A few things to know before you start:

- **Race is recorded only as Black or white.** The data includes no one else.
- **Counts are top-coded:** "10 or more" prior felony arrests is stored as text. `parse_number()` turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
- **`Residence_PUMA`** is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia's PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can't map it.
- **`Training_Sample`** is NIJ's own train/test split. Use it.

# Part 1: Load and clean


```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(pROC)
library(knitr)

nij <- read_csv("data/assignment6/nij_recidivism.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(
    recid = as.integer(Recidivism_Within_3years == "Yes"),
    male = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years = factor(Prison_Years,
      levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                 "Greater than 2 to 3 years", "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma = factor(Residence_PUMA),
    education = factor(Education_Level),
    dependents = parse_number(Dependents),
    prior_violent = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Violent),
    offense = factor(replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing"))
  )
train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)
```

**1.1** How many people are in `train` and in `test`? What share of each was rearrested within three years?

```{r}
#| label: samples
sample_summary <- tibble(
  sample = c("Train", "Test"),
  n = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  rearrest_pct = 100 * c(mean(train$recid), mean(test$recid))
)
kable(sample_summary, digits = 2)
```

**Answer:** There are 18,028 training records and 7,807 test records. Their three-year rearrest rates are 57.80% and 57.42%, respectively.

**1.2** Look at `Gang_Affiliated`. How many values are missing, and who are they? (Hint: cross-tabulate it with `Gender`.) What would happen to your sample if you added this variable to a model without handling the missing values?

```{r}
#| label: missing-gang
gang_missing <- nij %>%
  mutate(gang_missing = is.na(Gang_Affiliated)) %>%
  count(Gender, gang_missing)
kable(gang_missing)
```

**Answer:** The 3,167 missing gang-affiliation entries all belong to women. Using this field without handling its missing values would remove women from model fitting and leave them without test predictions.

# Part 2: What would you know at the moment of decision?

The parole decision happens **at release**. Some columns in this file were recorded **during** the three years of supervision that followed.

**2.1** Sort every predictor column into one of two lists. You don't need code; use `names(nij)` and the column names.

| Known at release | Recorded during supervision (leakage) |
|---|---|
| `Gender`, `Race`, `Age_at_Release`, `Residence_PUMA`, `Gang_Affiliated`, `Supervision_Risk_Score_First`, `Supervision_Level_First` | `Violations_ElectronicMonitoring`, `Violations_Instruction`, `Violations_FailToReport`, `Violations_MoveWithoutPermission` |
| `Education_Level`, `Dependents`, `Prison_Offense`, `Prison_Years` | `Delinquency_Reports`, `Program_Attendances`, `Program_UnexcusedAbsences`, `Residence_Changes` |
| `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Violent`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Property`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Drug`, `_v1`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_DVCharges`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_GunCharges` | `Avg_Days_per_DrugTest`, `DrugTests_THC_Positive`, `DrugTests_Cocaine_Positive`, `DrugTests_Meth_Positive`, `DrugTests_Other_Positive` |
| `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Felony`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Misd`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Viol`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Prop`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Drug`, `_v2`, `_v3`, `_v4` | `Percent_Days_Employed`, `Jobs_Per_Year`, `Employment_Exempt` |
| `Prior_Revocations_Parole`, `Prior_Revocations_Probation` |  |
| `Condition_MH_SA`, `Condition_Cog_Ed`, `Condition_Other` |  |

`ID`, `Training_Sample`, and the four `Recidivism_*` outcome columns are excluded from both predictor lists. Derived variables keep the timing of their original fields. Race is recorded at release but is excluded from the model.

The opaque CSV headers follow the positions in the [NIJ codebook](https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/recidivism-forecasting-challenge-appendix-2-codebook.pdf): `_v1` is prior arrest probation/parole violations, `_v2` prior conviction probation/parole violations, `_v3` prior domestic-violence convictions, and `_v4` prior gun-charge convictions. I treat the initial supervision fields as available at release, subject to checking their timestamps in actual use.

**2.2** Pick one variable from the right-hand column and explain, in two sentences, why including it would make your model look better than it really is.

**Answer:** `Percent_Days_Employed` is accumulated after release. It would give the model information that is unavailable when the parole decision is made, overstating what it could predict at that time.

# Part 3: Build a race-blind model

Start from this model.

```{r}
#| label: base-model
base_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests,
                family = binomial, data = train)

summary(base_fit)
```

**3.1** Exponentiate the coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for `prior_fel_arrests` in one sentence, using the word *odds* correctly.

```{r}
#| label: odds-ratios
odds_ratios <- tibble(term = names(coef(base_fit)),
                     odds_ratio = exp(coef(base_fit)))
kable(odds_ratios, digits = 3)
```

**Answer:** With the other variables held fixed, one more unit in the recorded felony-arrest count is associated with odds multiplied by 1.182, or 18.24% higher odds of rearrest. The count is top-coded, and this is not an 18.24-point probability increase.

**3.2** Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use `predict(..., type = "response")` with `newdata` to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

- a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
- a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person's probability? Why are the two changes different?

```{r}
#| label: probability-change
people <- tibble(
  male = c(1, 1),
  age_group = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)
people_more <- people %>% mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests + 1)
probability_change <- tibble(
  age_group = people$age_group,
  probability_two_arrests = predict(base_fit, newdata = people, type = "response"),
  probability_three_arrests = predict(base_fit, newdata = people_more, type = "response")
) %>% mutate(change_percentage_points =
               100 * (probability_three_arrests - probability_two_arrests))
kable(probability_change, digits = 4)
```

**Answer:** For the younger man, predicted risk rises from 56.45% to 60.51% (+4.06 percentage points). For the older man, it rises from 17.86% to 20.45% (+2.59 points). Logistic regression applies a constant change to log-odds, so the probability change depends on the starting risk.

**3.3** Improve the model. Add at least **three** predictors from your "known at release" list. Keep race out. Call it `my_fit`. In two or three sentences, say what you added and why you expected each one to help.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check for missing values before you add a variable
Some columns have blanks: `Prison_Offense` is missing for about 1 in 8 people, and `Supervision_Level_First` for about 1 in 15. If you add one as it is, `glm()` **silently drops** those people from training, and `predict()` returns `NA` for them in `test`. Then `mean()` gives `NA` in Parts 4–6, and `table()` quietly leaves them out. Either leave the variable out, or keep the blanks as their own category, for example `mutate(offense = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing"))`. Whichever you choose, say so in your answer.
:::

```{r}
#| label: my-model
my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests +
                education + dependents + prior_violent + offense,
              family = binomial, data = train)
stopifnot(nobs(my_fit) == nrow(train))
```

**Answer:** I included education and dependents to describe circumstances before release, plus prior violent arrests and prison offense to distinguish types of criminal history. I expected these to add information beyond total arrests and age. Offense blanks are kept in a “Missing” category; the other chosen fields are complete, so every training record is retained.

# Part 4: Choosing a threshold

**4.1** Add a column `p_hat` to `test` with predicted probabilities from `my_fit`, and a column `pred_50` that flags anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

```{r}
#| label: confusion
test <- test %>%
  mutate(p_hat = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
         pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5))
confusion <- table(Actual = factor(test$recid, levels = 0:1),
                   Predicted = factor(test$pred_50, levels = 0:1))
confusion
rates_at <- function(data, threshold) {
  pred <- as.integer(data$p_hat >= threshold)
  tp <- sum(pred == 1 & data$recid == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred == 1 & data$recid == 0)
  tn <- sum(pred == 0 & data$recid == 0)
  fn <- sum(pred == 0 & data$recid == 1)
  tibble(threshold = threshold, n = nrow(data),
         high_risk_pct = 100 * mean(pred == 1),
         rearrest_pct = 100 * mean(data$recid == 1),
         tp = tp, fp = fp, tn = tn, fn = fn,
         sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn), specificity = tn / (tn + fp),
         fpr = fp / (fp + tn), fnr = fn / (fn + tp))
}
rates_50 <- rates_at(test, 0.5)
kable(rates_50 %>% select(high_risk_pct, rearrest_pct, sensitivity, specificity), digits = 3)
```

**Answer:** At 0.5, sensitivity is 81.75% and specificity is 46.03%. The confusion matrix has 3,665 true positives, 1,794 false positives, 1,530 true negatives, and 818 false negatives.

**4.2** What share of the test set does your model label "high risk" at 0.5? Compare it to the share actually rearrested. What does that tell you about 0.5 as a default for this data?

**Answer:** The model flags 69.92% of the test sample, while 57.42% were rearrested. Its false-positive rate is 53.97%, so the default cutoff would impose substantial extra supervision on people who were not rearrested.

**4.3** Compute sensitivity and specificity for every threshold from 0.30 to 0.80 in steps of 0.05, and plot both lines on one chart with threshold on the x-axis.

Hint: in the lab you called `rates_at()` three times by hand. Here you need eleven thresholds. `map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) ...)` runs the same code once per threshold and stacks the results into one data frame. Your version will need `p_hat` instead of `pred`, and `recid` instead of `two_year_recid`.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-sweep
thresholds <- seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.05)
threshold_results <- map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) rates_at(test, t))
kable(threshold_results %>%
        select(threshold, high_risk_pct, sensitivity, specificity, fpr, fnr), digits = 3)
threshold_results %>%
  select(threshold, sensitivity, specificity) %>%
  pivot_longer(-threshold, names_to = "metric", values_to = "rate") %>%
  ggplot(aes(threshold, rate, color = metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Classification threshold", y = "Rate", color = "Metric") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.4** Plot the ROC curve for `my_fit` on the test set with `pROC` and report the AUC. In one sentence: what does the AUC tell you, and what doesn't it tell you about the decision the department has to make?

```{r}
#| label: roc
roc_object <- pROC::roc(test$recid, test$p_hat,
                        levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
auc_value <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_object))
roc_points <- tibble(fpr = 1 - roc_object$specificities,
                      sensitivity = roc_object$sensitivities)
ggplot(roc_points, aes(fpr, sensitivity)) +
  geom_path(color = "#2166ac", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "False positive rate (1 - specificity)", y = "Sensitivity",
       title = paste("Test-set ROC; AUC =", round(auc_value, 3))) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Answer:** The test AUC is 0.704, showing the model’s ability to rank higher- and lower-risk records, but it does not establish calibration, select a policy threshold, or show that the resulting decisions are fair.

# Part 5: Is it race-blind?

Race isn't in your model. Now check the errors by race on the **test set**.

**5.1** At the threshold of 0.5, compute for each race: the share labeled high risk, the share actually rearrested, the **false positive rate** (labeled high risk, not rearrested, out of everyone not rearrested), and the **false negative rate**.

```{r}
#| label: race-rates
race_rates_at <- function(threshold) {
  map_dfr(sort(unique(test$Race)), function(race) {
    rates_at(test %>% filter(Race == race), threshold) %>%
      mutate(race = race, .before = 1)
  })
}
race_50 <- race_rates_at(0.5)
kable(race_50 %>% select(race, n, high_risk_pct, rearrest_pct, fpr, fnr), digits = 3)
```

**5.2** Repeat 5.1 at two other thresholds from your sweep. Does the gap between groups close, stay, or flip?

```{r}
#| label: race-thresholds
race_thresholds <- map_dfr(c(0.40, 0.70), race_rates_at)
kable(race_thresholds %>%
        select(race, threshold, n, high_risk_pct, rearrest_pct, fpr, fnr), digits = 3)
```

**Answer:** The Black-minus-white false-positive gap is 12.07 percentage points at 0.40 and 3.73 points at 0.70; it is 10.34 points at 0.50. The gap narrows at the higher cutoff but stays positive. Black false-negative rates remain lower at all three cutoffs, so their direction does not flip.

**5.3** Investigate at least two candidates by comparing their distributions by race. Possibilities include age, prior arrests, prison offense, and place (`puma`). Show your evidence with a table or chart for each.

```{r}
#| label: proxy-evidence
prior_by_race <- test %>% count(Race, prior_fel_arrests) %>%
  group_by(Race) %>% mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(prior_fel_arrests, Race, pct) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Race, values_from = pct, values_fill = 0)
kable(prior_by_race, digits = 2,
      caption = "Prior felony arrests: percent within each race; 10 means 10 or more")

age_by_race <- test %>% count(Race, age_group) %>%
  group_by(Race) %>% mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(age_group, Race, pct) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Race, values_from = pct, values_fill = 0)
kable(age_by_race, digits = 2, caption = "Age at release: percent within each race")
```

**Answer:** Black parolees are younger in this test sample: 32.64% are under 28, versus 21.30% of white parolees. The coded mean prior-felony count is slightly lower for Black parolees (5.70 versus 5.84), despite differences elsewhere in the distributions. These comparisons show that inputs vary by race; they do not isolate the cause of the error gap.


# Part 6: Does it hold up in places it hasn't seen?

Use leave-one-PUMA-group-out cross-validation **on the training set**, the same recipe as Week 10's leave-one-district-out.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-cv
pumas <- levels(train$puma)
cv_puma <- map_dfr(pumas, function(u) {
  cv_train <- train %>% filter(puma != u)
  cv_test <- train %>% filter(puma == u)
  fit <- glm(formula(my_fit), family = binomial, data = cv_train)
  stopifnot(fit$converged, nobs(fit) == nrow(cv_train))
  cv_test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(predict(fit, newdata = cv_test, type = "response") >= 0.5)) %>%
    summarize(puma = u, n = n(), share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"),
              accuracy = mean(pred == recid),
              fpr = mean(pred[recid == 0] == 1),
              actual_negatives = sum(recid == 0))
})
```

**6.1** Plot each PUMA group's false positive rate against its share of Black parolees. What pattern, if any, do you see?

```{r}
#| label: puma-plot
ggplot(cv_puma, aes(share_black, fpr)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#2166ac", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = puma), nudge_y = 0.01, size = 3,
            check_overlap = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Share of Black parolees in held-out PUMA group",
       y = "Held-out false positive rate", size = "People",
       title = "Leave-one-PUMA-out validation on the training set") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Answer:** The 25 held-out groups have false-positive rates from 43.37% to 63.27%. Their correlation with the share of Black parolees is 0.382, suggesting a positive association with considerable variation. This uses training records only, and the smaller groups have less precise rates.

**6.2** If you put `puma` itself into the model as a predictor, would that make the model more or less race-blind? Make an argument using what you found in 6.1. (You may test it, but you don't have to.)

**Answer:** PUMA would supply a location-based proxy for group composition, so I would consider it less race-blind in the information it uses. The area validation shows an association with errors, but a model comparison would be needed to establish whether adding PUMA increases or decreases the racial error gap. It would also create an unseen-category problem when predicting a completely held-out PUMA.

# Part 7: The memo

Write a memo (**400–600 words**) to the Department of Community Supervision. It must:

1. **Pick a threshold for Use A and a threshold for Use B**, and defend each using the cost of a false positive and a false negative *in that use*. Cite your own numbers from Parts 4 and 5.
2. Tell them **whether "the model doesn't use race" means it treats Black and white parolees the same**, using your Part 5 results.
3. End with one sentence: **"I would / would not deploy this for Use ___, unless ___."**

Write to a deputy commissioner, not to a statistician. No code, no jargon you haven't explained.

For restrictive supervision, I would consider a cutoff of 0.70; for priority reentry support, I would start with 0.40. The consequences of a wrong flag are different in these two uses. Neither cutoff is an established optimum, because we have not been given service capacity or a formal cost for each kind of mistake.

Under Use A, a false positive means extra restrictions for someone who was not rearrested. Reporting requirements and monitoring can interfere with work and family responsibilities. At 0.50, this happens to 53.97% of people who were not rearrested, or 1,794 people in the test sample. At 0.70, that falls to 16.43%, or 546 people. The tradeoff is serious: the higher cutoff misses 60.50% of those who were rearrested. Those missed flags may represent lost opportunities for oversight, but the data do not show that extra supervision would prevent rearrest. I would therefore evaluate the higher cutoff as a possible review trigger rather than automatically impose restrictions.

For Use B, overlooking someone who might benefit from housing or employment assistance is a different concern. A 0.40 cutoff reaches 91.35% of those rearrested and misses 8.65%; the missed share is 18.25% at 0.50. However, 82.12% of the whole test sample would receive priority, making staffing and service capacity important. People flagged who were not rearrested would also use resources. Some may still need help, since rearrest is not a direct measure of housing or employment needs. A lower score should therefore not prevent someone from requesting voluntary support.

The race promise needs qualification. At 0.50, 72.56% of Black people and 66.27% of white people are flagged. Among those who were not rearrested, the rates are 58.41% and 48.07%. At 0.70 these false-positive rates decrease to 18.03% and 14.30%, but remain unequal. At 0.40 they are 74.86% and 62.79%. Applying one cutoff to everyone does not remove group differences. The input distributions differ by race, and arrest history also records contact with enforcement. Simply removing the race column does not remove those relationships.

The model has a test AUC of 0.704, indicating some ability to rank risk without demonstrating reliable individual probabilities. When each area was left out of training, false-positive rates in that area ranged from about 43% to 63%. The records also concern releases in 2013–2015, so performance should be checked on recent data before use. I would review group-specific errors, provide human review, and evaluate whether services actually improve outcomes. The proposed cutoffs should be confirmed in a new sample because this test set was used to examine them.

I would not deploy this for Use A, unless an independent pilot demonstrates acceptable racial error gaps, meaningful review and appeal, and benefits sufficient to justify the added restrictions.

# Optional challenge (no extra points. just extra muscles.)

`Supervision_Risk_Score_First` is the score Georgia's existing risk tool assigned at the start of supervision. Treat a score of 7 or higher as "high risk" and compute its false positive rates by race on the test set. Does the state's current tool look better or worse than yours?

```{r}
#| label: optional-benchmark
benchmark <- test %>%
  mutate(existing_high_risk = as.integer(Supervision_Risk_Score_First >= 7))
benchmark_results <- benchmark %>% group_by(Race) %>%
  summarise(total = n(), score_missing = sum(is.na(existing_high_risk)),
            scored_nonrearrested = sum(recid == 0 & !is.na(existing_high_risk)),
            false_positives = sum(existing_high_risk == 1 & recid == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            fpr = false_positives / scored_nonrearrested, .groups = "drop")
benchmark_shared <- benchmark %>% filter(!is.na(existing_high_risk)) %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
    existing_fpr = mean(existing_high_risk[recid == 0] == 1),
    model_fpr = mean(pred_50[recid == 0] == 1),
    existing_fnr = mean(existing_high_risk[recid == 1] == 0),
    model_fnr = mean(pred_50[recid == 1] == 0), .groups = "drop")
kable(benchmark_shared, digits = 3)
```


**Answer:** Among people with an available state score, the state tool's false-positive rates are 37.25% for Black people and 33.81% for white people. On these same records my model's rates are 58.42% and 47.93%, but its false-negative rates are much lower. The state tool has fewer false alarms at its chosen cutoff, rather than clearly better performance on every measure; 145 missing scores are excluded from this matched comparison.

## AI assistance

AI helped with coding, checking calculations, and drafting text. The reported results come from running my model on the NIJ data; the final interpretation and submission remain my responsibility.
